titleStmt.title: Delay Efficient Real-time Multicast Scheduling in Multi-hop Wireless Sensor Networks

analytic.title: Delay Efficient Real-time Multicast Scheduling in Multi-hop Wireless Sensor Networks

div.p: We study real-time multicast scheduling in multihop wireless sensor networks. Given multiple heterogeneous periodic multicast tasks, for each task, the data produced by the distinguished source node for a certain control application with sufficiently long time horizon need to be delivered to all target nodes periodically, the objective is to design an interferenceaware routing and scheduling protocol to meet the delay requirements. In this work, we propose an efficient distributed routing and scheduling protocol under the protocol interference model. We conduct schedulability analysis and the proposed protocol approximately optimize the schedulable load. Based on our protocol design, we propose schedulability test schemes for a set of real-time multicast tasks. The performance evaluation results corroborate our theoretical analysis.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Multicast is a fundamental communication task in multihop wireless sensor networks (WSNs). In many applications such as news dissemination and multimedia applications, the multicast tasks come in a periodic fashion. It is envisioned that a distinguished source node generates data and multicasts data to a set of target nodes periodicaly. Furthermore, for the successful adoption of WSNs, a delay constraint is imposed in most real-time multicast scheduling applications.

In this work, we study real-time multicast scheduling problem. It is described as follows. Consider a distinguished source node and a collection of target nodes, the source node issues a set M of periodic multicast tasks with deferred deadlines. Each task M i ∈ M has a period p i and a subset of target nodes. There is a relative deadline requirement d i for each target node to receive the data. Each task also has an initial release time a i , thus, the j-th instance (or the job at the t-th period) of a task M i will be released at time a i +(j-1)•p i , and all the target nodes of the task M i expect to receive the corresponding data within the time a i + (j -1) • p i + d i . Let a transmission schedule consists of the node activities on when to transmit packets and what packets to transmit. Under the protocol interference model [10], the objective is to jointly design routing and a conflict free schedule of activities for all nodes to finish multiple periodic multicast tasks. To the best of our knowledge, all existing work focus on one-shot multicast while we address multiple heterogeneous periodic multicast tasks.

Compared with prior work, our main contributions are the scheduling protocol design, schedulability test, and performance evaluation. Given multiple heterogeneous periodical multicast tasks in WSNs, we design joint routing and scheduling protocols under the protocol interference model. Using the insight from the protocol design, we propose both necessary conditions and sufficient conditions for schedulability of a set of multicast tasks in WSNs. We demonstrate that the proposed protocols achieve a total load that is at least a constant fraction of the optimum load. The performance evaluation results corroborate our theoretical analysis.

div.head: Related Works:
div.p: Multicast has been well studied in multihop wireless networks such as capacity maximization [1], [13], energy-efficient network routing [5], [18]- [20], and maximizing lifetime [9], [16].

On the other hand, a lot of real-time scheduling algorithms has been proposed in the literature such as [15] and references therein for both single node case and multiple node case. Among them, Earliest Deadline First (EDF) scheduling and Rate Monotonic (RM) scheduling are the most representative classes of scheduling algorithms. As pointed out in [14], EDF achieves a utilization of exactly one and RM is optimum among all scheduling methods with fixed priorities. However, there are only a few papers on real-time scheduling in multihop wireless networks for different group communication patterns such as data aggregation [2], [3], [22] and data collection [12], [21].

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section II formulates the periodic multicast scheduling problem. Section III provides preliminaries for the proposed protocol design. Section IV focuses on protocol design on the periodic multicast scheduling problem. Section V provides schedulability result on multicast. Section VI presents the performance evaluations. Section VII concludes the paper.

div.head: II. PROBLEM FORMULATION
div.p: Consider a WSN deployed in a two-dimensional Euclidean plane, all sensor nodes have a uniform transmission range and a uniform interference range, both of which are normalized to one. The communication graph of the WSN is modeled as a graph G = (V, E) which is a Unit Disk Graph (UDG) [4]. In the UDG G, an edge -→ uv ∈ E exists if and only if the Euclidean distance uv between two nodes u and v in V is at most one. Under the protocol interference model [10], a 978-1-4799-5952-5/15/$31.00 ©2015 IEEE communication link -→ uv ∈ E is able to transmit successfully if the receiver node v is not within the interference range of any other concurrent transmitter node.

Let s be a distinguished source node. Assume the source node s issues a set M of periodic multicast tasks. Each task M i ∈ M has a subset V i ⊆ V of target nodes. We assume that the multicast task M i has a period p i . For each task M i , the source node s will generate periodically a data unit to be multicasted to the target nodes in V i . We assume that it will take χ i time to transmit a data unit of task M i over any link. We assume that χ i could be different for different tasks. The multicast task M i will be initially released at time a i , thus, the j-th instance, denoted as M j i , of the task will be released at time a i + (j -1) • p i . Each task M i has an end-to-end delay requirement r i for the target nodes in V i to receive the answer. Thus, the deadline for all the target nodes in V i to receive the answer is
div.formula: f j i = a i + (j -1) • p i + r i .
div.p: Due to the network delay, we allow r i ≥ p i for the task M i .
We formulate the main problem to be studied as follows: consider multiple heterogeneous periodic multicast tasks

each with its own period p i , processing time χ i , end-to-end deadline f i , and a set of target nodes V i ⊂ V , the objective is to test whether the set of tasks are satisfied and if yes, design an effective routing and scheduling protocol to meet the deadline requirements under the protocol interference model. In the presence of a routing structure, a transmission schedule is to assign a time to each node for each packet such that if every packet is transmitted according to the schedule via the routing structure, the target nodes of each task receive the corresponding data within a certain delay.

The end-to-end delay of the schedule for a multicast task is defined as the maximum difference between the time when any instance of any multicast task is released and the time when all the target nodes receives the required data for this instance. i.e., for the j-th instance of a task M i , we use t J u to denote the assigned transmission time to a packet p J for the job J of j-th instance of M i at node u; the end-to-end delay of j-th instance for M i is d i,j = max{t J u -(a i + (j -1) • p i ) : ∀J, ∀u}, and the end-to-end delay of M i is d i = max j d i,j . We require that ∀i, d i ≤ r i .

Note that for some multicast task M i ∈ M, the data unit may have a large size. Thus, we need to split the large data unit into multiple packets, and transmit one packet each time. We assume that time is divided into time-slots and the transmission of a packet costs one time-slot. Then, we have χ i ∈ N, where χ i represents the transmission time of a data unit for task M i . When transmitting multiple packets of a large data unit, we allow perfect preemption which means that we are allowed to interleave packets from different multicast tasks. However, we assume that preemption only occurs at the end of a time-slot.

div.head: A. Scheduling for One-shot broadcast Task
div.p: We first review the one-shot broadcast problem [7], [8], [11] that will be used in the protocol design in Section IV-B. Consider a communication graph G = (V, E) and a source node s and the set V of all target nodes, a broadcast schedule is represented by S = {t u : u ∈ V } such that if each node u forward a message at the time-slot t u , then all nodes in V receive the single message. Here {max u t u : u ∈ V } is called the delay of the broadcast schedule. The objective is to find a conflict-free feasible broadcast schedule S = {t u : u ∈ V } with minimum delay. The one-shot broadcast problem or (called minimum latency broadcast schedule) has been extensively studied such as [11]. Since most protocol designs are based on the concept of Connected Dominating Set [6], [18] in a graph, let us define it first.

In a graph G = (V, E), a subset V 0 ⊆ V is a dominating set (DS) if each node in V is either in V 0 or adjacent to some node in V 0 . Nodes in V 0 are called dominators, whereas nodes not in V 0 are called dominatees. A subset C ⊆ V is a connected dominating set (CDS), if C is a dominating set and C induces a connected subgraph. Lemma 1: [11] For the one-shot broadcast problem, there exists a conflict-free schedule S : V → N + with delay at most R + O(log R). Here R is the radius of the graph.

For every schedule S given in Lemma 1, every node u in the associated CDS is assigned with a time-slot t u . We observe a property on the assigned time-slots to nodes in the CDS. The difference between assigned time-slots for any two conflicting nodes is at most a constant.

div.head: Lemma 2:
div.p: In the schedule S given in Lemma 1, for any pair of nodes u, v in the CDS with assigned time-slots t u and t v respectively, if |t u -t v | ≥ C, then the transmissions of node u and v will not conflict with each other. Here C = 31.

div.head: B. Single-hop Multi-Task (SMT) Scheduling
div.p: Let us consider a special case of the periodic multicast scheduling problem. Each task requires only single-hop transmissions. This means that, for each period of a task, just a single-hop transmission is enough.

To be formal, we define the problem of single-hop transmission scheduling for multiple tasks with preemption allowed. Consider a set of periodic tasks M ⊆ M where each task M i ∈ M only requires single-hop transmissions. Each packet p J is assigned with a time-slot J u and has delay d i ≤ r i (assume J comes from task M i , the objective is assign each packet p J at node u a time-slot J u . Here preemption for SMT means that: during the transmissions of multiple packets of a single data unit for some task, we may insert other urgent transmissions to meet the deadline requirement. Note that for SMT, due to the absence of network delay, we set r i = p i for each task M i ∈ M.

For SMT, we introduce two well-known methods, i.e., RM and EDF scheduling [14], [17]. a) RM scheduling: We define the request rate of a task as the reciprocal of its corresponding period, i.e. γ(M i ) = 1/p i : ∀M i ∈ M. Then RM is simply described as follows. A task with higher request rates will be assigned with higher static priorities. RM ensures that each packet to be transmitted before deadline if the following two constraints are satisfied.

div.head: 1) each input for SMT has utilization of at most n•(2 1/n -1).
div.p: Here the utilization can be seen as the summation of all tasks' request rates Mi∈M χ i • γ(M i ) in SMT and n is the number of tasks that are involved in SMT. For large n, we obtain the utilization bound of 69% which means that as long as each input has utilization of at most 69%, all packets are able to make their deadlines. 2) for each task, the delay requirement is at least its period.

Given the value of C, for RM scheduling, we observe the following property. Lemma 3: Given a task set M u , assume the utilization is at most 0.69 C , there exists a scheduling J u for each job instance J such that ∀J, C| J u (i.e., C divides J u ). Proof: This can be verified as the task set has a utilization of at most 0.69 C . Let us assume that the period is greater than C here. If each packet will cost C consecutive time-slots instead of just one time-slot, then the task set has utilization of at most 0.69. By using RM scheduling, we obtain a schedule such that each packet is scheduled with C consecutive time-slots and has delay at most its corresponding period. From each packet p J u , we select the time-slot J u among the C consecutive time-slots such that C| J u (C divides J u ). b) EDF scheduling: Using EDF, priorities are assigned to tasks according to the deadline of their current packets. A packet will be assigned the highest priority if the deadline of its current packet is the nearest, and will be assigned the lowest if the deadline of its current packet is the farthest. For EDF scheduling, Lemma 4 holds. div.head: A. Overview
div.p: The protocol consists of three phases. In the first phase, for each task M i ∈ M, construct a routing tree T i rooted at the distinguished source node of the network. In the tree T i , if a node u is a parent of a node w, then u is responsible for transmitting data to w. Note that, T i is a Steiner Tree connecting the terminals of V i ∪ {s} where s is the distinguished source node and V i is the set of target nodes for the periodic task M i .

In the second phase, we specify the data units to transmit for each node at current time. For each task M i ∈ M with a multicast tree T i , during each period, every node in T i adds one data unit to its buffer upon receiving the data unit from its parent in T i for this period of task M i .
In the third phase, we assign concrete time to every packet from every node's buffer to transmit.
We then describe the details of each phase separately.

div.p: Assume the communication graph is G = (V, E), we select a CDS T CDS of G by using an existing distributed approach [18]. We then construct a spanning tree T G by connecting each node not in the CDS to a neighboring dominator.

The pruning operations result in a routing tree T i for each task M i ∈ M.
2) Assigning data units for each node: After constructing routing trees for all multicast tasks, we specify data units to transmit for each node u periodically.
First of all, observe that a node u is involved with a task M i ∈ M if and only if u ∈ T i . We denote the set of tasks that node u is involved with as M u .

For any task M i , if node u is involved with M i (M i ∈ M u ), during each period p i , the node u needs to add a data unit for M i to its buffer. The data unit is either original or a relayed data. In the former case, u is just the source node. In the latter case, u is a relay node and it needs to wait until receiving the corresponding data from its parent before adding data to its buffer.

3) Node and packet scheduling: After the second phase, each node contains data units in real time in its buffer. Here a data unit may consist of several packets. To sum up, we present the protocol design in Algorithm 1. We will prove in Section IV-C that Algorithm 1 is interferencefree and at the same time, achieves an end-to-end delay which is bounded by a constant factor of the optimum solution.

div.head: C. Performance Analysis of Our Schedule
div.p: We first prove the correctness of our schedule. This means that the schedule avoids wireless interference and at the same time, every node will transmit strictly after it receives the packet from its parent, for each j-th instance of task M i . We then prove our schedule has bounded delay. Note that the proofs hold when J u is computed by either RM or EDF scheduling in Section III-B. Next, we propose another schedulability test scheme such that if we are not able to pass the test, we definitely cannot satisfy the set of periodic multicast tasks. For a multicast task M i ∈ M, it costs the source node χ i time-slots to receive data during every period p i . Obviously, for a set of tasks M, the initial load at source node v s , given by Mi∈M χi p i , cannot exceed one if the set M of tasks are satisfied. Theorem 7: The gap between the proposed sufficient condition (Theorem 5) and necessary condition (Theorem 6) for schedulability test is bounded by a constant C.

div.head: VI. PERFORMANCE EVALUATIONS
div.p: We randomly deploy a set of n nodes with transmission range 50 in an area of size 400 × 400. We always keep that the network is connected. There is a communication link if |uv| ≤ 50 for an arbitrary pair of nodes u and v. Each link has a quality variable which scales with the link length. The source node will generate up to 20 tasks.

The main flow of performance evaluation is as follows. Firstly, the distinguished source node initiates to construct multicast routing trees (based on the CDS) which cover all nodes. Secondly, the source node generates a set of tasks and multicasts them to the targets nodes one by one with different periods. A task will be considered as unfinished if any target node of this task cannot receive the packet in more than 3 periods. We now evaluate the performance of Algorithm 1 in different scenarios. In the first one, we vary the network size from 10 to 100 with 10 steps. For each task, we pick target nodes randomly. Figure 1 shows the simulation results. The success ratio is equal to the number of successful rounds divided the total rounds for existing tasks.

When the number of nodes increases over 40, the success ratio will quickly drop from around 0.8 to 0.2. This is mainly caused by capacity bounds of any CDS. The new packets from newly increased nodes lead teh CDS to be saturated such that many packets are dropped due to the buffer limit. In the second scenario, we fix the number of nodes to 100 and increase the number of target nodes (destination nodes) in each task from 5 to 50 with 10 steps. The figure 2 shows the success ratio under various amount of target nodes. When the number of target nodes is small (less than 25), most of tasks are satisfied. When the number of target nodes is larger than 25, the success ratio dropped quickly. Both simulation results show that Algorithm 1 performs well in terms of stability.

div.head: VII. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: We jointly designed a routing strategy as well as a packet scheduling protocol for periodic multicast tasks in multihop wireless sensor networks. We theoretically prove that the proposed protocol achieves constant approximation in terms of schedulability. Based on our protocol design, we propose both necessary conditions and sufficient conditions for schedulability of a set of multicast tasks. For the future work, we will study the real-time multicast scheduling problem under other wireless interference models and under cognitive radio networks.
